title: The death of a friend (4.4–4.9)
hookLine: his closest friend dies and everything becomes death to him
tomorrow: after a grave like that, is it safe to love again?

cards: Some people keep a friend's number in their phone long after the funeral, and never quite delete the thread. Augustine would understand.

Back in his hometown, a young teacher now, he had a friend he grew up with, who shared his studies and his ideas. That friendship, he says, was sweeter to him than anything else in his life then. Who was he?
The Confessions never gives his name. Then the friend falls ill with a fever, and lies unconscious, and his family does something Augustine doesn't expect.

teach.b: They have him baptized. Augustine, who had led him away from the faith, assumes it means nothing, and when the friend wakes, he jokes about it.
The friend turns on him, he says, as if he were an enemy, and tells him to stop if he wants to stay his friend.
Augustine holds back, meaning to bring it up later. There is no later. A few days on, the fever returns, and his friend dies while Augustine is away.

In Pusey's words: "At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death." His hometown became a torment. He looked for his friend everywhere, and every place only said he wasn't coming.
He became a great question to himself, he says, and only weeping was sweet.
Looking back, he borrows an old poet's phrase for a friend, "half of my soul," and says it felt like one soul in two bodies.

Here's the part to tell someone tonight: the friend's last real conversation with Augustine was a rebuke, defending a baptism Augustine had laughed at. The older Augustine, writing to God, doesn't hide it.
He also sees what had gone wrong in the loving, and that's where tomorrow picks up.

how: Catholics pray for those who have died, have Masses offered for them, and remember them together on All Souls' Day.

games.q: what does “the death of a friend” mean?
o: a beloved friend's death that turned all to grief
a friend who moved away to another city
a quarrel that ended a friendship for good

p: rebuked him, as if from an enemy
an old poet's phrase for a friend

s: the Confessions tells us the friend's name
he is never named. Augustine calls him half of his soul.
the friend defended his baptism when Augustine joked about it
he turned on Augustine as if from an enemy and told him to stop.
Augustine says grief like that is a sign of weak faith
he describes it without shame: whatever he looked at was death.

games.q: a teammate's older brother died last month, and she says everything at school reminds her of him. what does Augustine's book give her?
o: words for it: whatever he looked at was death, because he loved.
a rule: grief that lasts this long means faith is weak.
a fix: stay busy, and the reminders will stop mattering.
games.why: Augustine describes a hometown where every place said his friend wasn't coming. he doesn't scold the grief; he names it.

practice: Close your eyes and remember a friend who has died, or anyone dear you've lost, and let one ordinary detail come back: a laugh, a phrase, the way they said your name.
Stay with it gently, without hurrying the grief along or pushing it away. If you pray, you can commend them to God by name; if not, just keep the detail company until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The death of a friend. Augustine's grief for the friend of his youth, when everything he looked at was death, and half his soul seemed gone.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 4.4: whatever I looked at was death.

carryVoice: Your line: half of my soul, the name grief gives to love that has nowhere to go. Be gentle tonight.

sources.q: At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death.
